statuteCitation: Ohio Revised Code Chapter 5312 (Ohio Planned Community Law) and Chapter 5311 (Ohio Condominium Act)
deadline: Hearing must be requested in writing no later than the tenth day after receiving the notice (R.C. 5312.11(D))

introParagraph: If your Ohio HOA has hit you with a fine you believe is unfair, you have powerful legal protections under Ohio law. The Ohio Planned Community Law (R.C. Chapter 5312) and Ohio Condominium Act (R.C. Chapter 5311) require associations to follow strict procedures before imposing or collecting fines. Many Ohio homeowners receive fines that are procedurally defective, exceed the association's authority, or violate the recorded declaration. A well-drafted dispute letter that cites the correct Ohio statutes can stop collection, force the HOA to schedule a proper hearing, and often resolve the issue without litigation. This page explains your rights and helps you generate a customized demand letter.
lawExplanation: Ohio regulates HOA fines primarily through Ohio Revised Code § 5312.11, which governs enforcement assessments (fines) in planned communities. Before an HOA can impose an enforcement assessment, R.C. § 5312.11(C) and (D) require the board to: (1) give the owner a written notice describing the violation, stating the proposed amount, stating the right to a hearing before the board and how to request it, and giving a reasonable date to cure a continuing violation if a cure opportunity applies; (2) hold a hearing if the owner delivers a written request no later than the tenth day after receiving the notice, with at least seven days' written notice of the hearing; and (3) refrain from levying the assessment before that hearing. The assessment must be imposed in accordance with the declaration (R.C. § 5312.11(A)). For condominium associations, R.C. § 5311.081(C) sets a parallel notice, hearing, and cure procedure before enforcement assessments are levied. Ohio courts have consistently held that HOAs must strictly comply with both their governing documents and statutory notice requirements. Homeowners may also challenge fines that are arbitrary, discriminatory, or selectively enforced. A violation of the chapter, the declaration, the bylaws, or the rules is grounds for a civil action for damages or injunctive relief and an award of court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (R.C. § 5312.13; R.C. § 5311.19 for condominiums), and an owner who shows that a charge was improperly charged in an action to discharge a lien may be awarded attorney's fees (R.C. § 5312.12(D)). Properly levied enforcement assessments can also become part of the association's lien (R.C. § 5312.12). Understanding these statutory protections is essential before paying any disputed fine.
letterStrategy: A strong Ohio HOA fine dispute letter accomplishes several goals at once. First, it creates a written record showing you formally objected within the statutory window — critical if you later need to defend against a lien or lawsuit. Second, it forces the board to confront specific procedural failures: missing written notice, no opportunity to cure, no hearing offered, or fine amounts not authorized by the recorded declaration. Citing R.C. § 5312.11 (or § 5311.081(C) for condos) by section number signals that you understand your rights and are prepared to enforce them. Third, the letter should formally request a hearing before the board, preserving your due process rights under the statute. Fourth, it should demand production of the specific declaration provision, bylaw, or rule the HOA claims you violated, along with proof the rule was properly adopted and recorded. Many Ohio HOA fines collapse at this stage because boards cannot produce authority for the rule or evidence of proper adoption. The letter should also raise selective enforcement if neighbors with similar conditions were not fined. Finally, the letter should warn that continued collection efforts on an improperly assessed fine — including liens, late fees, or attorney's fees added to your account — will be challenged and that you will seek recovery of your own attorney's fees under R.C. § 5312.13 if litigation becomes necessary. A well-cited, professional letter often results in the fine being withdrawn without further dispute.
proceduralNotes: Larger disputes or requests for injunctive relief must be filed in the Court of Common Pleas. Ohio's general statute of limitations for breach of contract (which covers declaration violations) is six years for written contracts under R.C. § 2305.06. Mechanics of HOA liens are governed by R.C. § 5312.12, and homeowners must act quickly if a lien has been filed. Mediation is often required or encouraged by HOA governing documents before litigation. Keep copies of all correspondence and send your dispute letter via certified mail, return receipt requested.

faq.q: Can my Ohio HOA fine me without a hearing?
faq.a: No. Under R.C. § 5312.11, an Ohio planned community HOA must provide written notice of the violation, an opportunity to cure (if applicable), and notice of your right to a hearing before the board. If you request a hearing in writing, the HOA must hold one before imposing or collecting the fine. Fines imposed without these procedural steps are generally unenforceable. Condominium associations face similar requirements under R.C. § 5311.081(C). If your HOA skipped these steps, your dispute letter should specifically cite the missing procedure.

faq.q: How long do I have to dispute an HOA fine in Ohio?
faq.a: You should request a hearing in writing as soon as possible after receiving the notice of violation. Under R.C. § 5312.11(D), the written request must be delivered to the board no later than the tenth day after you receive the notice, and the right to a hearing is waived if you miss that date. Even if a deadline has passed, you can still dispute the underlying validity of the fine, especially if proper notice was never given or the declaration does not authorize it. Send your dispute letter by certified mail to create a documented timeline.

faq.q: Can my Ohio HOA put a lien on my home for unpaid fines?
faq.a: Possibly, but only if the fine was properly imposed under R.C. § 5312.11 and the lien complies with R.C. § 5312.12. Under that section the association's lien covers assessments and charges levied under R.C. § 5312.11 that remain unpaid ten days after they become due, and it takes effect when the association files a certificate of lien with the county recorder. Liens based on procedurally defective fines can be challenged: R.C. § 5312.12(D) lets an owner sue in the court of common pleas to discharge a lien for amounts improperly charged, and the court may award attorney's fees to the owner. If you receive a lien notice, dispute it immediately in writing.

faq.q: Can I recover attorney's fees if I win an HOA fine dispute in Ohio?
faq.a: In many cases, yes, but not through a single prevailing-party clause. A violation of Chapter 5312 or the governing documents is grounds for a civil action for damages or injunctive relief and an award of court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (R.C. § 5312.13), and in an action to discharge an improper lien the court may award the owner attorney's fees (R.C. § 5312.12(D)). R.C. § 5311.19 provides a similar civil action for condominium disputes. Mentioning your intent to seek attorney's fees in your dispute letter often motivates HOA boards to reconsider.

faq.q: What if my HOA is selectively enforcing rules against me?
faq.a: Selective or discriminatory enforcement is a strong defense under Ohio law. HOA boards owe homeowners a duty of good faith and must enforce rules consistently. If neighbors have similar violations (same fence color, same landscaping, same parking situation) and were not fined, document this with photos and dates. Raise selective enforcement in your dispute letter and demand the HOA explain why you were singled out. Ohio courts have invalidated fines where boards could not justify inconsistent enforcement, and this is often grounds for the fine to be withdrawn.
